title: First results from PADRE/MeDDEA: X-rays from a flare and its CME

abstract_screen.rationale: Uses STIX flight-spare detectors on MeDDEA and joint STIX/Fermi GBM/ASO-S HXI/AIA spectral and imaging analysis of a flare and its CME. It bears directly on flare HXR spectroscopy, nonthermal electrons and energetics, and cross-calibration of STIX-like data, though timing/QPPs are not the focus.

problem.explanation: The paper is about flare electron energetics and HXR emission from flare versus CME. It touches electron acceleration and transport but not rapid variability, QPPs or energy-dependent timing.

method.explanation: It uses STIX spectral fitting (thermal + thick target), STIX CLEAN/MEM imaging, light-travel-time correction and inter-instrument light-curve comparison, with Python sunkit-spex fitting. These methods transfer directly, though no time-series or periodicity methods are used.

data.explanation: STIX is central: occulted spectra, images and light curves, plus AIA, HXI and GBM. It introduces MeDDEA, which carries STIX-identical detectors, gives 0.5 s cadence and offers an open Python pipeline.

phenomenon.explanation: The subject is nonthermal electrons and thermal plasma in a large flare, the Neupert-like heating of the high coronal source and decay timescales set by trapping and conduction. The focus on CME-associated emission is somewhat off-centre.

future.explanation: MeDDEA gives an Earth-view STIX-like spectrometer for stereoscopic timing and spectral comparison of flares, especially occulted ones. Its high-cadence event lists could support timing or QPP work, and the occulted-flare approach can be applied across the STIX catalogue.

one_line: First science paper from the PADRE/MeDDEA CubeSat spectrometer, which carries STIX flight-spare CdTe detectors: it cross-calibrates MeDDEA against ASO-S/HXI and Fermi/GBM to within ~10% (18–30 keV) for the M6 flare SOL2025-11-28T22, and uses STIX's 15°-occulted view to show that CME-associated nonthermal HXR flux is ~1% of the flare flux while its thermal energy is comparable.
summary: The authors analyse the first large flare seen by MeDDEA (GOES M6, 28 Nov 2025). From Earth the flare was on the limb but visible; for Solar Orbiter/STIX it was occulted by 15° (occultation height 24.5 Mm). Spectral fitting with sunkit-spex (MeDDEA) and OSPEX (STIX, HXI, GBM) gives thermal-plus-thick-target fits. MeDDEA photon fluxes agree with HXI and GBM to 1.01±0.10 in 18–30 keV, after an ad hoc 5.0 s clock correction. The occulted STIX source has a nonthermal flux 0.95%±0.15% of the flare flux, the same spectral index (δ≈5.2), a cooler temperature (~13 MK vs ~29 MK) and comparable thermal energy (~4–6×10^29 vs 2.4×10^29 erg, filling factor 1). STIX CLEAN images (sub-collimators 7–10) show the source moving at ~450 km/s with the AIA 131 Å erupting flux rope. The occulted light curve is less impulsive and decays more slowly, and its thermal emission rises during the nonthermal burst in a Neupert-like way. For the researcher, the value lies in the STIX spectral/imaging workflow, the multi-instrument timing comparison, and a new STIX-cross-calibrated, high-cadence, Earth-view HXR data source with Python tooling. QPPs and fine timing are not addressed.
offers: A worked example of a STIX occulted-flare spectral analysis with the newest STIX calibration (Massa et al. 2026, sswidl v0.6.2) and light-travel-time correction (+48.3 s) (Sect. 2.1, 3.1).
MeDDEA photon event lists with Python tools: data on the SDAC umbra server and the padre_meddea GitHub repo; spectra fitted with sunkit-spex via its custom-spectrum tutorial (Sect. 2.2).
A cross-calibration benchmark: MeDDEA/HXI 1.02±0.07 and MeDDEA/GBM 0.94±0.11 in 18–30 keV (Fig. 4).

A multi-instrument HXR spectrogram and light-curve comparison including Konus and Aditya-L1/HEL1OS, with notes on GBM pileup (detector N0) and HXI entrance-window effects on apparent timing (Figs. 1–2).
Table 1: flare versus high-corona T, EM, volume, thermal energy, density and δ, useful as a reference for energetics.

findings.evidence: The MeDDEA 28–70 keV light curve at 0.5 s cadence has ~9% errors at peak. A 5.0 s clock shift was required to align MeDDEA with HXI and GBM nonthermal peaks (Sect. 3.1, Fig. 2).
findings.inference: MeDDEA can supply sub-second nonthermal light curves for M-class flares. Its absolute timing is not yet reliable, so any cross-instrument timing analysis (e.g. STIX–MeDDEA lags) would need independent clock verification.
findings.recommendation: If MeDDEA is used for timing comparisons with STIX, align it on a reference instrument (GBM/HXI) and check the status of the MeDDEA clock correction before interpreting second-level delays.

findings.evidence: The HXI 10–20 keV curve peaks and decays before MeDDEA's because HXI's thicker entrance window shifts its mean photon energy higher. The thermal HXR curves peak before GOES/XRS (Sect. 3.1).
findings.inference: Apparent timing differences between instruments in nominally identical energy bands can come from instrument response rather than physics. This matters for energy-dependent timing studies that combine STIX with other instruments.
findings.recommendation: Compare in photon space or forward-model through each instrument's response when doing multi-instrument energy-dependent timing.

findings.evidence: The occulted STIX 12–25 keV profile has a similar onset but is less impulsive and decays more slowly than the flare. The occulted 4–12 keV emission rises during the nonthermal burst, Neupert-like. This is interpreted as trapping, with conductive losses weaker in the high corona (Sect. 3.1, Fig. 2).
findings.inference: Comparing occulted and unocculted temporal profiles can separate coronal-source variability from footpoint variability. That is relevant to locating where flare variability (including any QPPs) originates.
findings.recommendation: Consider occulted STIX events with Earth-view HXR coverage as a way to isolate coronal-source temporal behaviour from ribbon emission.

findings.evidence: The occulted nonthermal flux is ~1% of the flare flux, with identical δ≈5.2 in the thick-target fit. The thick- versus thin-target choice is argued from a density estimate (~2×10^9 cm^-3) and is left unresolved (Sect. 3.3, 4).
findings.inference: This is a quantitative constraint on how the electron population is partitioned between flare and eruption. The interpretation is model-dependent, especially for thin-target or coronal sources.
findings.recommendation: Treat the 1% fraction as thick-target-specific. When fitting coronal STIX sources, test both thick- and thin-target models.

findings.evidence: EUI was at 6-minute cadence and missed the impulsive phase, so it was excluded (Sect. 3.4).
findings.inference: EUI cadence during non-campaign periods can limit joint STIX/EUI timing studies. Event selection needs to check EUI cadence, for example by favouring Major Flare Campaign periods.
findings.recommendation: Screen candidate events for EUI high-cadence modes before building STIX–EUI timing case studies.

reading.why: Defines the occulted STIX plus Earth-view HXR method, the occultation-height formula and the comparison event.

reading.reference: Massa et al. 2026, Solar Physics 301 (STIX calibration)
reading.why: The newest STIX calibration, essential for any STIX spectral work.
STIX imaging of occulted flare coronal sources using coarse sub-collimators.

reading.reference: Christe et al. sub. to A&A 2026 (MeDDEA instrument)
reading.why: Needed to judge MeDDEA modes, decimation, livetime and timing before using its data.
Catalogue and temporal properties of occulted flares.
Validates sunkit-spex against OSPEX, which supports a Python-based spectral workflow.

caveats: Single-event study: no QPP, periodicity or energy-dependent timing analysis is performed.
The MeDDEA clock needed an ad hoc 5 s correction, and cross-calibration is only validated in 18–30 keV.
Thermal energies assume a filling factor of 1 and ignore systematic volume uncertainties. The volume estimates for the CME source differ by a factor of 2.
The 1% electron fraction rests on the thick-target assumption.
EUI data were not used, so there is no direct STIX–EUI connection.
The CME focus is partly outside the researcher's core flare-variability interests.
events: SOL2025-11-28T22:20 M6 (limb flare, 15° occulted from Solar Orbiter, narrow ~700 km/s CME)
